nodes.body: Perch Lane is holding a house clearance: three trestle tables of other people's belongings standing out in the drizzle. In a shoebox of oddments lies a tin whistle, its mouthpiece gone dull green. Scratched into the barrel, so faint it only shows when tilted, are six small marks with a wavy line running underneath them.

choices.label: Open the case and read the card.

nodes.body: Inside the case is a card, folded into eighths and soft as cloth. Spidery ink on it says THE ROUNDS. Below that are six place names from an old Padgett that barely exists now. The last name is BANDSTAND. There is also a row of six numbers, with four of them crossed out. Mrs Okonjo runs the clearance. She says the box came from Perch Lane. She says the man who lived there once played in the old town band.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Okonjo about the house.
Start at the nearest mark on the barrel.
Take the card to the library.

nodes.body: Mrs Okonjo has cleared eleven houses in Padgett this year. She remembers every single one. The paperwork for this house sits in a folder in the van. The house belonged to a man called Harold Vine. He died in March. There is one box of his things that has not been priced yet.

choices.label: Ask to see the unpriced box.
Look at the photographs properly.
Ask to look round the house itself.

nodes.body: Hold the whistle up to the light, and you'll see the wavy line on the barrel is the river, with six marks sitting along it. But they are in a different order than the order on the card. The nearest mark is fifteen minutes away, pointing to the old weighbridge. That is a car park now, where a ticket machine stands in place of the old scales.

choices.label: Go to the weighbridge car park.
Follow the wavy line along the river.
Look at the iron bridge.

nodes.body: The library keeps Padgett's local history on two shelves. There is also a microfilm reader that eats twenty pence coins. Aisha works behind the desk. She has been waiting almost a year for someone to ask her a question with a real date in it.

choices.label: Work the local history shelf.
Get the microfilm reader going.
Ask Aisha what she already knows.

nodes.body: The unpriced box sits under the seat of the van. Inside it is a band cap with a green band. There are also two photographs with names written on the back. A paper wallet holds receipts for reeds, valve oil, and one repaired euphonium.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the band cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: Two black and white photographs show a band standing on some steps in Padgett, twenty-one people in caps. On the back, in soft pencil, are eleven names and the words FIRST SATURDAY. The steps in the picture are not the town hall steps, and are not anywhere obvious.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the band cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: The house in Perch Lane stands empty, its key hanging on a hook in the van. There are rules about who may go inside and when. Mrs Okonjo will say yes to someone who asks properly, and a flat no to anyone who wanders in through the back.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the band cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: The weighbridge is forty parking spaces and a ticket machine now. All that is left of it is a strip of iron set into the tarmac, and a wall carrying a rectangle of cleaner brick, where something the size of a paperback was taken off and never put back.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the chip shop.

nodes.body: The wavy line on the barrel runs from the iron bridge down to the weir. The six marks sit along it at distances that match no modern map of Padgett at all, until somebody draws the filled-in mill leat back in.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the chip shop.

nodes.body: The iron bridge has been painted green, over green, over green. On its upstream side is a plate that reads PADGETT 1903. Beside it is a small square of bare rivets. A second, smaller plate used to be there. It is clearly missing now.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the chip shop.

nodes.body: Two shelves, one of them a run of parish magazines with soft, worn spines. In the December 1961 issue is a paragraph about the Rounds that lists all six stops, in an order that does not match the card in the case.

nodes.body: The microfilm reader eats twenty pence pieces and holds the Padgett Gazette back to 1878. Every December, the paper carries a photograph of the band standing somewhere in the snow, their instruments held like something breakable.

choices.label: Look at the plate in the drawer.

nodes.body: Aisha has sat behind that desk for four years, and she keeps a drawer full of things people brought in and never picked up. Inside it is a brass plate wrapped in a freezer bag, the size of a paperback book, with four holes in it. No one has ever explained what it is.

choices.label: Look at the plate in the drawer.

nodes.body: Eleven names sit on the back of a photograph. Three of them are still on doorbells in Padgett, and one is painted across the front of the chip shop. A name on a photograph is not a person until somebody goes and knocks on a door.

nodes.body: A receipt is a dull document that cannot lie: valve oil in 1989, a euphonium repaired in 1994, and a locksmith called out to the store under the bandstand in November 1998, six weeks before the band played for the last time.

nodes.body: A plate painted over five times is still a plate. You can see the difference in slanted light, or by feeling it with your thumbnail. On this route, there are two walls where the paint sits on top of a shape, instead of lying flat. One of these walls is behind a menu board.

nodes.body: The chip shop wall has a menu board screwed on. It sits at exactly the height where a plate would be. Deniz has never once looked behind it. The shop is packed with customers from four until eight. Between those times, it is completely empty.

nodes.body: The clearance is set for Friday. The contractor is already booked. Once a store is cleared, it stays cleared. Whatever is under the bandstand will go into a lorry, then into a skip. No one in the room will ever know what it was.

choices.label: Go and see Mr Vance at the parks depot.

nodes.body: Harold Vine played second cornet for thirty-one years. He kept every receipt he was ever given. When he died, he left behind a house with one shelf of music. There were no photographs on the walls. The neighbours knew his name, but not much else. That says something about a person, too.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock.
Count what the six figures must be.
Take everything to Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: Bill Hurst was the last bandmaster. He lives above the old bakery. Everyone who talks about him says the same two things. First, he is not what he used to be. Second, you should ask him anyway.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to hold the clearance.

nodes.body: There is only one afternoon left before the house is emptied. There are three places worth checking. The top of the wardrobe. The back of the meter cupboard. And the gap behind the bottom drawer. That gap is where people in every house hide the thing they do not want thrown out.

choices.label: Ask about the cage at the depot.
Get into the chapel.

nodes.body: The card lists six places. The barrel marks them in a different order. Only one of these two orders is the order the band really walked. The other order was written down later, by someone sitting at a table.

nodes.body: The bandstand sits at the top of the park. Its paint is flaking off. Under it, a steel door is set into a brick arch. A six-figure combination padlock hangs on the door. It is green with age. Someone tried to open it with a screwdriver, but gave up.

nodes.body: Six stops, six plates, one figure on each, and a six-figure padlock on a steel door. Four of the figures on the card are crossed out in the same ink as the rest, which means somebody tried and got them wrong, rather than used them and moved on.

nodes.body: Mr Vance runs parks and grounds. He works out of a yard behind the leisure centre. He has a clipboard, a van, and a contractor booked for Friday morning. Twice this year, people above him have said that everything in that store is rubbish.

nodes.body: The last Rounds ran on the first Saturday of December 1998, in sleet. The Gazette gave it four column inches and a photograph of eleven people, where there had once been twenty-one.

nodes.body: The number on the minutes rings a desk. That desk has changed departments twice. The person who answers is friendly but cannot help. They can only tell you the one person who might be able to.

nodes.body: The unpriced box goes into a general lot on Thursday. A dozen other boxes go with it. By the time anyone understands what was inside, things are gone. The cap, the photographs, and the receipts have gone to three different counties. The whistle stays. The card stays too. But everything else that could prove anything is gone.

The six marks turn out to be six real places. Walking between them takes two hours in the rain. It answers nothing at all. There are four bare walls, a car park, and a padlock. It is a very good map of a town that has moved on. The card goes back into the case.

ending.title: Six Marks and a Wet Afternoon

nodes.body: By five to five, there is a folder. It holds the six stops, the dates, the minutes, and a photocopy of the plate. It is truly good work. The lorry still comes on Friday. The folder goes onto the local history shelf. Somebody will find it in twenty years and wonder.

The door under the bandstand is steel, set in a brick arch. The padlock is a six-wheel combination lock, gone green with age. The first two wheels turn freely. The last four wheels turn stiffly. This fact is worth more than any guess.

choices.label: Walk down to the river and think.

nodes.body: Five people give five different answers about where the third Round stood. Each one sounds sure. The afternoon is spent trying to choose between them. By the time anyone thinks to check a printed page, the library has closed. Only Thursday is left.

The form goes in on Wednesday, is acknowledged on Wednesday, and read on the following Tuesday, four days after a lorry, two men and a skip have made the question academic. The acknowledgement is polite, and arrives in an envelope with a window in it.

There are five plates and five figures. Their order depends on one thing: did the Rounds run clockwise, or did they run the way the card lists them? These two orders disagree in three places out of six.

nodes.body: The third order is the one the parish magazine printed in 1961. It opens the lock at twenty past seven on Thursday evening. Two residents are there, along with a notebook. A man of eighty-four stands on the grass behind them. For a moment, nobody says anything at all.

It takes an hour with a cloth and a bottle of valve oil, and then Bill Hurst plays eight notes on the bandstand steps. It is Thursday evening, and six people watch him. Three almshouse windows open across the park, and they stay open until he stops.

On the Friday morning the lorry was booked for, the head teacher signs for a bass drum, four horns, a cornet, and two music stands. The lorry takes only the real rubbish, and nothing else. By the following summer, there is a school band. It is not very good yet.

The store is emptied on schedule, but a list is made first. So four cases, a minute book, and a box of photographs come out before the skip does. Everything else goes. It is not the week anybody hoped for. But it is not the week that would have happened without the list, either.

The six figures are a date, written the way a bandmaster would say it: the first Saturday in December, 1961. Once you see that, you cannot un-see it. It is also seen at ten past nine on Friday morning. That is one hour and ten minutes after the lorry.

No one in charge is standing in the park on Friday morning. The folder sits in a bag on a kitchen table across town. The store is empty by twenty past eight. The padlock seemed like the whole problem, but it never really was.
Padgett has eleven instruments, a room, and one evening a week free. All it needs now is one adult willing to be in charge, but that last thing is still missing. Someone has to ask for it out loud.

The name in the cornet case belongs to a grandmother who lives on the next street, and she played the cornet until she was nineteen. She has kept that secret for fifty years. She takes the case back home, and two weeks later, she brings it to a practice.

A minute book from 1934, four hundred photographs, a run of programmes, and one card headed THE ROUNDS, accessioned, numbered, and on a shelf with a date stamp on the back of every sheet. Aisha puts the whistle photograph in the case by the door.

Deniz leaves the plate uncovered and moves the menu board a foot to the left, and for about a month people come into the chip shop to look at a piece of brass and buy chips while they are there. Then they stop, and the plate stays.

ending.title: The Plate Under the Menu Board

nodes.body: The story runs on Friday. It sits under a photo of an empty store and a skip. It is good writing about something that already happened. Four people write in. They say they would have helped, if only someone had asked them on Tuesday.

There are eleven players, one borrowed drum, a photocopied map, and six brass plates. The band stops at all six spots in the cold. They play badly at each one. More people follow along than anyone expected. Half of them are under twelve.

Forty people walk the route on a Saturday in October. They follow a man who is eighty-four years old. He stops at each plate and tells what once stood there. At the weighbridge, there is no plate at all. Still, everyone stands in the car park and listens anyway.

Five plates go back onto five walls, each with the right screws. A man in the industrial estate cuts a new sixth plate from brass. He will not take any money for it. The new plate goes onto the car park wall. It fits into the rectangle that has been waiting for twenty-eight years.

ending.title: Six Plates Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: The whistle goes back into the case with the card folded into eighths beside it, and lives on a shelf, played badly about once a week. It is the only object in the story that ends up exactly where it started, and means something completely different.

ending.title: The Whistle Goes Back in Its Case

nodes.body: Instruments to the school, paper to the library, photograph to the almshouses, plates to the walls, and the card to the archive with a note saying who found it. It takes three weeks of small dull errands, and nothing is left in a bag under anybody's bed.

The store comes out onto the grass. It gets listed and photographed. Then it is divided into keep and skip. Two men watch, paid by the hour. They are surprisingly interested. By the end of the week, the room under the bandstand is swept, dry, and empty.

The skip leaves the park at nine on Friday morning, carrying a bass drum and four cases. Someone takes a photo of it leaving, from the gate, but the Gazette will not print it. There is simply nothing to say about it.

Three grown-ups could have stopped it, but no one told them. On Wednesday, asking felt like a big deal. By the next Monday, it did not feel so big at all. All three grown-ups agreed, one after another.

The last order is wrong. The wheels go back to zero. The trail started at a shoebox in Perch Lane. It passed through six walls and sixty years. Now it ends at a steel door in a cold park. A truck is booked for the morning.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
